title: Getting a cast
what: A plaster or fiberglass cast is put on your arm or leg. It holds the bone or ligaments still while they heal.
why: For fractures, hairline cracks, bad sprains and torn ligaments, or after some surgeries.
duration: putting it on usually takes 15 to 30 minutes; you usually wear it for several weeks, as your doctor says
tell_doctor: Skin conditions or wounds in that area
If you are pregnant, before an X-ray

prepare.title: Clothing
prepare.text: Loose clothes that will fit over the arm or leg in a cast.

prepare.title: Jewelry
prepare.text: Take rings and bracelets off the injured arm. It may swell.

bring: X-rays, if they were taken elsewhere
Wide trousers or a loose sleeve
steps: Usually an X-ray is done first
The doctor puts the bone or joint in the right position
The skin is covered with a soft sleeve and a layer of padding
Wet plaster or fiberglass bandages are wrapped on
The cast is smoothed to the shape of your arm or leg
A follow-up X-ray is often done
feel: Warmth as the cast sets. This is normal
The injury may ache for the first few days
after: For the first 1 to 2 days, keep the arm or leg raised. This reduces swelling
Keep the cast dry: cover it with a plastic bag when washing
Do not push anything under the cast, even if it itches
Wiggle your fingers or toes, if you can
Go for a checkup and X-ray when your doctor tells you
red_flags: Fingers or toes turn blue, white, cold, or numb: see a doctor right away or call emergency services
Severe pain that keeps getting worse, or the cast presses too hard
A bad smell, burning, or wetness under the cast
Pain and swelling in the calf: see a doctor right away

faq.q: What can I do if it itches under the cast?
faq.a: Do not push anything inside. You can blow cool air in with a hair dryer.

faq.q: Can I stand on a leg in a cast?
faq.a: Only if your doctor allows. Usually you use crutches at first.

reminders.text: Cast soon. Take off rings and bracelets, and bring loose clothes.
